U_G = −GMm/r is negative and larger in size than K for a bound orbit, so E = K + U < 0. To escape, E must be raised to zero or above.
options: Right: it does not have enough energy to reach infinity.
Positive total energy means the object escapes.
Zero total energy is exactly the escape condition.
U is negative and adds to K.

why.correct: For a circular orbit K = ½mv² = GMm/(2r), so doubling r halves K (and v falls by √2).
options: Right: K = GMm/(2r) ∝ 1/r.
A larger orbit is slower: v = √(GM/r).
K goes as 1/r, not 1/r².
The orbital speed depends on r.

why.correct: E = −GMm/(2r): a larger r makes E less negative, that is, larger. The rocket bursts supply that energy. The satellite ends up slower, with less K but much more U.
options: Right: E = −GMm/(2r) is less negative at larger r.
It does move more slowly, but E = −K becomes less negative.
The rocket does work on it from outside the satellite-planet system.

why.correct: E stays constant because only gravity, a conservative force inside the system, acts. Falling inward, U = −GMm/r becomes more negative, so K and the speed increase.

why.correct: In a circular orbit, gravity points to the center and the velocity is tangent to the circle, at 90° to it. A perpendicular force does no work, so K and the speed stay constant; U is constant too, since r is.
options: Right: no work, no change in K.
Gravity pulls it toward the planet all the time.
